problemStatement.plain: The known proofs of f(k) → ∞ use algebraic height theory (Schinzel 1987, Schinzel-Zannier 2009). Is there a purely combinatorial proof via sumset bounds?
whyMatters: A combinatorial proof would bypass deep algebraic machinery
Would connect polynomial squaring to additive combinatorics

proven: For nonneg-coefficient polynomials, support(P²) = support(P) + support(P) exactly
|A + A| ≤ |A|² (trivial upper bound on sumset size)
Coefficient cancellation is the fundamental obstacle for general polynomials
open: Can cancellation be bounded sublinearly in |A + A| for general polynomials?
Is there any connection between Freiman-Ruzsa theory and cancellation control?

knowledge.markdown:
# Knowledge Base: erdos-485-oq-02

## Problem Understanding

The open question asks whether f(k) → ∞ can be proved combinatorially (via sumsets) rather than algebraically (via height theory).

## Key Results

1. support(P²) ⊆ support(P) + support(P) — always holds
2. For nonneg coefficients, equality holds → termCount(P²) ≥ 2k-1
3. Cancellation barrier: mixed-sign coefficients can eliminate sumset elements

## Dead Ends

- Direct sumset bounds fail for general polynomials due to cancellation

## Status (S3 STATE-SYNC 2026-05-16)

Erdos485OQ02.lean is COMPLETE (10 theorems, 0 sorries, 0 axioms). Mathlib v4.26.0 now provides Cauchy-Davenport and Plünnecke-Ruzsa — see sessions/session-003-statesync-mathlibgap-stale.md for refactor recipes.
